subject: English
passage: The Polished Tongue is a 1687 comedy by Felix Graves, written during the late Restoration period in England. At the time, fashionable gentlemen known as 'wits' prided themselves on their clever turns of phrase and ornate compliments, which they delivered in drawing rooms and coffeehouses to demonstrate their refinement. In the play, Graves satirizes these wits as having an exaggerated sense of their own cleverness, as seen when the character ______
prompt: Which choice most effectively uses a quotation from The Polished Tongue to illustrate the claim?

choices.A: Sir Reginald, who admires the wits from afar, urges his nephew, "If you would prosper at court, you must learn to speak as they do, and never let a plain word escape your lips."
choices.B: Sir Reginald says of the wits' favorite gathering place, "There assemble men who, for the price of a flattering ear, will spin you a compliment so tangled that you must thank them twice before you discover whether you have been praised or insulted."
choices.C: Lord Witmore, a celebrated wit, instructs a young admirer, "Mark me well, for whensoever I deliver a phrase of any consequence, you must commit it instantly to memory, lest so rare an ornament be lost to the world."
choices.D: Lord Witmore, a celebrated wit, complains of his young admirer, "I have never met a duller pupil, nor one so unfit for polite company; he stumbles over the simplest pleasantry and forgets a jest the moment it is spoken."

explanation:
Choice C is the best answer because it most effectively uses a quotation to illustrate the claim that Graves satirizes wits as having an exaggerated sense of their own cleverness. In the quotation, Lord Witmore, who is described as a celebrated wit, instructs a young admirer to memorize his phrases at once 'lest so rare an ornament be lost to the world.' By calling his own phrases 'rare ornaments' worthy of preservation, Lord Witmore reveals an inflated regard for his own verbal brilliance, directly illustrating the satirical portrayal described in the passage.

Why B is incorrect:

Choice B is incorrect because the quotation presents Sir Reginald describing the wits and their convoluted compliments from an outsider's perspective. Although the description mocks the wits' style, it doesn't show a wit character directly displaying an inflated sense of his own cleverness.
